passage: The substitute teacher was trying to shout over the construction noise next door, and nobody could hear her anyway. Kiran turned in his seat. "Hey, Salma Samosa," he whispered, loud enough for the row. Two boys snorted. Salma kept her head down. Kiran watched her ears go red. At break he nudged her elbow so her juice spilled, then said "Oops" with a grin. More laughter. The substitute was busy with the register and didn't see. Before home time, Kiran hid Salma's bag behind the cupboard. She searched, her lip trembling. Nobody told her where it was. Kiran felt the whole row looking at him, and a warm, powerful feeling spread through his chest.

qa.q: Where did Kiran hide Salma's bag?
qa.a: He hid it behind the cupboard.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when the row looked at him?
qa.a: He felt a warm, powerful feeling, enjoying the attention and the laughter.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage, and to whom?
qa.a: Any classmate or the substitute could stop the small acts now, by telling Kiran to stop or reporting it, before he learns that teasing pays and moves to worse.

qa.q: What is it like for Salma when nobody tells her where the bag is?
qa.a: She likely feels alone and ashamed, as if the whole row is against her.

grounding: It shows a boy testing a classmate with a nickname, a nudge and a hidden bag while watching for reactions and an audience that laughs.

passage: On the first day after the Puja holidays in Kolkata, Arnab sat behind Kalyani in class 5. When she answered a question slowly, he muttered, "Tortoise," and looked around. Nobody laughed. He tried again in the queue, bumping her shoulder. Kalyani turned, surprised. A couple of boys grinned this time. By the end of the week he had a routine: "Tortoise" when she walked in, her pencil box knocked to the floor, her water bottle moved to the dustbin. Each time, he checked who was watching. Each time more children giggled, and no one said stop. Arnab walked taller in the corridors. He was already thinking about what he could do on Monday.

qa.q: What nickname did Arnab give Kalyani?
qa.a: He called her "Tortoise."

qa.q: How can you tell Arnab wanted an audience?
qa.a: He looked around after the first nickname and checked who was watching each time, walking taller and feeling proud as the giggles grew.

qa.q: What went wrong in the class, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Nobody said stop, so Arnab learned the teasing earned him attention; a classmate or teacher stepping in early and telling a trusted adult could break that pattern.

qa.q: How might Kalyani be feeling by the end of the week?
qa.a: She is probably confused and hurt, turning in surprise at first and now facing a daily routine of mockery with no one helping. 😢

grounding: It illustrates a boy starting with a nickname, a bump and moved belongings, watching for reactions and moving to more when others laugh and nobody stops him.

passage:
The school bus was stuck behind a wedding procession for half an hour, and Varun was bored.

He looked at Neelam two seats ahead, the girl who stammered when she read aloud. He'd called her "Ne-Ne-Neelam" once last week, just to see. A few boys had laughed. Nobody had said anything.

Today he said it again, louder. Three boys laughed this time. Neelam stared out of the window.

Varun watched her ears go red. He watched the boys watching him. Nobody told him to stop. The driver had the radio on.

Then he reached over and took her water bottle and passed it to the back seat. More laughter.

Varun leaned back, grinning. It was easy. It worked. He was already thinking about what he could do tomorrow.

qa.q: What was the school bus stuck behind?
qa.a: A wedding procession.

qa.q: How did Varun feel when the boys laughed and nobody stopped him?
qa.a: He felt pleased and powerful, learning that the cruelty was rewarded with attention.

qa.q: What could have stopped this from growing?
qa.a: A classmate saying "stop", or the driver or a teacher stepping in, so Varun learned the cruelty did not pay; Neelam telling an adult that day would also help.

qa.q: What is it like for Neelam with her ears going red?
qa.a: She feels humiliated and helpless, staring out of the window while others laugh.

grounding: Varun tests Neelam with a nickname and taking her bottle, watching for reaction and audience, and learns from the laughter that cruelty pays.

passage:
In the colony park after school, Gautam noticed that Chetan always sat on the same bench with his comic.

On Monday, Gautam called him "Chashmish" because of his thick glasses. Two boys snickered. Chetan pushed his glasses up and kept reading.

On Tuesday, Gautam nudged him off the end of the bench "by accident." A few more laughed.

On Wednesday, Gautam hid Chetan's school bag behind the slide, and watched him search the park, face getting pinker. Six children were watching now, giggling. None of the mothers on the far bench looked up.

Gautam felt taller than he had in weeks.

That night he planned Thursday. Something bigger.

qa.q: Where did Gautam hide Chetan's school bag?
qa.a: Behind the slide.

qa.q: What does Gautam feeling "taller than he had in weeks" show?
qa.a: It shows he feels powerful and proud, enjoying the attention the teasing brought.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could change it?
qa.a: Nobody stopped the small acts, so Gautam learned cruelty pays; an adult or friend stepping in early would change that lesson.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel searching for his bag?
qa.a: He is likely embarrassed and upset, his face getting pinker as others giggle.

grounding: Over three days Gautam tests Chetan with a nickname, a nudge and a hidden bag, and with an audience and no one stopping him, plans more.

passage:
"Santosh, why do you keep calling Jasleen 'Potato'?"

"It's just a joke, Manu."

"She doesn't laugh."

"Everyone else does. Watch." He raised his voice. "Oi, Potato! Nice lunch!"

A few kids at the next table giggled.

"See?"

"Yesterday you hid her pencil box."

"And she didn't even tell Ma'am. She just looked for it."

"So?"

"So nothing happens. Nobody says anything."

"That's not a reason to keep doing it."

"It's funny."

"It's not funny to her."

"Tomorrow I'm going to put her bag on the fan. That'll be even funnier."

Manu stood up. "Then I'm telling Ma'am. Now." He walked towards the staffroom. Santosh stopped grinning.

qa.q: What nickname did Santosh use for Jasleen?
qa.a: "Potato".

qa.q: How does Santosh feel when nobody says anything?
qa.a: He feels encouraged and bold, believing the cruelty pays because no one stops him and others laugh.

qa.q: What did Manu do right, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Manu refused to laugh and went to tell Ma'am straight away, which breaks the pattern of no one stopping Santosh.

qa.q: What might Jasleen be feeling as she searches for her pencil box without telling?
qa.a: She probably feels embarrassed and alone, maybe afraid that telling would make things worse.

grounding: In dialogue Santosh tests Jasleen with a nickname and hidden things, reading laughter and silence as permission, until a classmate goes to a teacher.

passage: In Class 4, I, Karthik, was the boy who gave Vishal his nickname: "Chashmish", because of his thick glasses. I said it once, softly, just to see. He went pink. A few kids laughed. So the next day I said it louder. Then I bumped his elbow in the lunch line, and when his dal spilled, the whole row laughed. Nobody told me to stop. The teacher was busy at her desk. By Friday I hid his school bag behind the water tank, and I felt like a king watching him search. Now I'm eleven and I understand: the laughing was what kept me going. Vishal never laughed once.

qa.q: Where did Karthik hide Vishal's school bag?
qa.a: He hid it behind the water tank.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel watching Vishal search for his bag?
qa.a: He felt powerful, like a king, because the laughing audience made the cruelty seem worth it.

qa.q: At what point could someone have stopped this, and how?
qa.a: On the very first day, when a few kids laughed at the nickname, a classmate or the teacher could have said stop and checked on Vishal before it grew.

qa.q: What was it like for Vishal during that week?
qa.a: Vishal was probably embarrassed and scared, going pink, losing his dal and searching for his bag, and he never laughed once.

grounding: Shows a child testing cruelty with a nickname, a nudge and a hidden bag, and learning from laughter and silence to go further.
